summary: This informational memo explains how to use the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm with XML Signatures. It allows signing data of any kind to provide integrity and authentication, whether the data is inside the XML or referenced from it.

plainLanguage.summary: A signature proves who wrote something and that it was not changed. This document explains how to sign XML files with a modern, compact kind of signature.

questions: how to use elliptic curves in xml dsig
how to sign xml with ecdsa
why use elliptic curves for signatures
subtitle: Using compact elliptic curve signatures to sign XML documents

tldr.problem: XML Signatures previously supported only RSA and DSA algorithms, which require large key sizes and produce large signatures, making them less efficient for bandwidth-constrained or resource-limited systems.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies how to use ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) with XML Signatures, defining the XML structures needed to represent ECDSA keys and signatures within the XML Signature framework.
tldr.outcome: Systems can now use ECDSA for XML signing, gaining smaller signatures, smaller keys, and faster operations while maintaining equivalent cryptographic strength.

today: RFC 4050 is an Informational RFC. The ECDSA XML Signature method it defines is now supported in various XML security implementations and is widely used where signature efficiency and key size matter.

sections.title: Introduction and ECDSA Advantages
sections.content:
XML Signatures [XMLDSIG] is a standard for digitally signing XML data. A signature proves that specific data has not been tampered with and authenticates who signed it. The original specification supported only two signature algorithms: RSA and DSA.

ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) is a modern public-key signature algorithm based on the mathematics of elliptic curves. Compared to RSA and DSA of equivalent strength, ECDSA offers three advantages: signatures are smaller, public keys are smaller, and operations are faster on many platforms. These benefits make ECDSA attractive for systems with bandwidth constraints, embedded devices, or applications where efficiency matters.
sections.plainLanguage: When you sign a document, you use a math trick that proves it is really from you and has not been changed. Modern signatures using elliptic curves are smaller and faster than old ones, so this document explains how to use them in XML.

sections.title: ECDSA and Domain Parameters
sections.content:
ECDSA produces a signature as a pair of numbers, conventionally called r and s. The algorithm uses a hash function (SHA-1) to digest the data being signed, then applies elliptic curve mathematics to create the signature. Domain parameters define the mathematical curve and field used: they specify which elliptic curve, its coefficients, a base point, and the order of that point.

ECDSA supports different types of fields: prime fields (simple integer arithmetic modulo a prime), characteristic two fields (arithmetic over binary polynomials), and odd characteristic extension fields. For each field type, domain parameters can be specified explicitly (by giving all coefficients) or by reference (by naming a well-known curve via an OID). The RFC defines XML structures to represent all of these variations, allowing interoperability between systems.
sections.plainLanguage: An elliptic curve is a specific mathematical shape. Different curves are used for different purposes, and you can either describe a curve completely or just refer to a famous one. The document shows how to write all this down in XML so computers can understand.

sections.title: Representing ECDSA in XML Signatures
sections.content:
The RFC defines an element called ECDSAKeyValue that goes inside the standard XML Signature KeyValue element, just like the existing RSAKeyValue or DSAKeyValue. The ECDSAKeyValue contains the public key (a point on the elliptic curve, with X and Y coordinates) and optionally the domain parameters.

The signature itself is the base64 encoding of the concatenation of the r and s values, as specified in the standard ECDSA definition. Signature validation uses the standard XML Signature canonicalization and comparison rules. The RFC specifies the algorithm identifier and namespace URI (http://www.w3.org/2001/04/xmldsig-more#ecdsa-sha1) so that implementations can recognize and process ECDSA signatures correctly.
sections.plainLanguage: The document shows exactly how to write an ECDSA key and signature inside an XML file so that any program can find and use them. It reuses the XML Signature framework that already exists, just adding the ECDSA pieces.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
ECDSA security depends on careful selection of key sizes and domain parameters. Key sizes must be appropriate: a 256-bit elliptic curve key provides roughly equivalent strength to a 3072-bit RSA key. The RFC references standards such as FIPS 186-2, ANSI X9.62, SEC 2, and IEEE 1363, which all provide recommended curves and key sizes proven to be secure.

Implementers MUST ensure that the curves and parameters they use are well-vetted and come from trusted sources. Poor parameter choices can leak the private key. The RFC recommends using named curves from established standards rather than generating custom parameters, as custom parameters are harder to validate and more prone to weaknesses. Proper key generation, secure storage, and protection of private keys are essential for maintaining the security of ECDSA signatures.
sections.plainLanguage: Using elliptic curves safely means picking the right size and using well-known curves that mathematicians have checked. Inventing your own curve is risky, so it is better to use ones that famous standards organizations have already tested.
